## Reading in Data w/ [palmerpenguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/articles/intro.html)

There are multiple options to read data into R

1.  Data download (manual click) -\> Move into project "data" folder -\> `read_csv()`
2.  Sometimes data is included in packages
    -   In this case, the penguins data we are going to analyze is included in the `palmerpenguins` package.
3.  Download via a URL

### Option 1

```{r, message=FALSE}

penguins_data <- read_csv("data/penguins_lter.csv")

```

### Option 2

There are two versions of data in this package.

```{r, message=FALSE}

penguins_data_from_package <- palmerpenguins::penguins

```

```{r, message=FALSE}

raw_penguins_data_from_package <- palmerpenguins::penguins_raw

## :: lets you reference a function in a package without loading the whole package
## :: is a referencing palmer penguins and requesting penguins_raw?
```

### Option 3

```{r, message=FALSE}
url_penguins <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/abcamp/CS201_FA26/main/data/penguins_lter.csv"

penguin_data_from_url <- read_csv(url_penguins)
```

Note that all of these methods of reading data in to R are *reproducible* meaning that this script should work for anyone using the appropriate steps.

## A Little Data Cleaning

Let's focus on the dataframe `penguins_data` for class purposes

-   If you click on the dataframe in your environment you'll notice the space in the column names, ex. `Culmen Length (mm)`

    -   Having spaces in column names often causes headaches, R doesn't like it, so we always avoid spaces

    -   Two common naming conventions are Snake Case and Camel Case

        -   Snake Case example: culmen_length_mm

        -   Camel Case example: culmenLengthMm

    -   There are other options!

![by Allison Horst](https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/dbb99049-2916-4bc8-824f-1816f5c4f06d_rw_3840.png?h=5c28a07483856cd07de35a50c772824d){fig-align="center"}

Lets start by cleaning one column name manually

First, with Base R

```{r, message=FALSE}

names(penguins_data)[names(penguins_data) == "Culmen Length (mm)"] <- "culmen_length_mm"

```

Second, with the `dplyr` package (part of `tidyverse`)

```{r, message=FALSE}

penguins_data <- penguins_data |>  
  rename(individual_id = "Individual ID")

```

We are lucky our penguins data frame only has 17 columns, but oftentimes data frames can have many more. So manually cleaning column names is highly inefficient.

Here is where the `janitor` package comes in handy!

```{r, message=FALSE}

penguins_data <- penguins_data |> 
  clean_names()

# clean_names makes the variables all lower case and turns the spaces into underscores
```

Now all of our column names are clean and our dataframe is ready for analysis! snake_case is the default, but others (like camelCase) are available. See documentation.

## Exploratory Analysis

The `skim()` function from the `skimr` package gives us a cool overview of the data with one line of code

```{r, message=FALSE}

summary(penguins_data)
#will produce different outputs for each column because the difference in type
# str columns will produce the N values, while int produces min, mean, med, max and quartile. quartiles are 4 equal parts

head(penguins_data)
#gives us preview for first few, will default to first 6 rows
#if you wanna see the first 10 rows: head(penguins_data, 10)
  #if you wanna see last 10 rows: tail(penguins_data, 10)

# *****
skim <- skimr::skim(penguins_data)
#shorter version of summary that lets you save it as a df
#turns variables(columns) from the og df into observations(rows)
# and summarizes each 

```

## Data Visualization

`ggplot2` is the most common package used for data visualization in R!

Let's start with the most basic plot we can make. Note that the **package** is `ggplot2` and the **function** we use is `ggplot`.

```{r, message=FALSE}
#can get rid of warning if you do this to code above ({r, message=FALSE})

ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) +
# what do we add here?

geom_histogram()

```

Cool! What if we color the histogram by species

```{r, message=FALSE}

ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram() 
  

```

Interesting! Seems like flipper length is very dependent on species of penguin

# Start here Friday

The magic of `ggplot2` is simplicity and *customization* so let's customize, based on these colors:

![](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/reference/figures/lter_penguins.png){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "darkorchid", "cyan4"), name = "Penguin Species") +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title = "Palmer Penguins' Flipper Length",
       subtitle = "Three Species observed on three islands in the Palmer Archipelago",
       x = "Flipper Length(mm)",
       y = "Number of Penguins")

#fill in the ggplot() adds color
#alpha adjust the color saturation of the bars
#name in the scale_fill_manual lets you change the legend
#

```

Manually choosing colors is cool, but there are also color palettes available for us with `viridis`

# Color Notes

```{r, message=FALSE}


ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", name = "Penguin Species")
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title = "Palmer Penguins' Flipper Length",
       subtitle = "Three Species observed on three islands in the Palmer Archipelago",
       x = "Flipper Length(mm)",
       y = "Number of Penguins")


```

Let's investigate flipper length with another type of data viz: a box plot!

```{r, message=FALSE}

ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(size = 0.5) +
 scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "magma", name = "Penguin Species") +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title = "Palmer Penguins' Flipper Length",
       subtitle = "Three Species observed on three islands in the Palmer Archipelago",
       x = "Flipper Length(mm)",
       y = "Number of Penguins") +
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust =1), legend.position = "none") 

#setup for the boxplot is the same as histogram
#boxplot needs x and y axis though
#geom jitter vs geom_point? might want to google the difference

#size = ? to adjust point size 
```

Again, let's customize! Add points for individual penguins.

```{r, message=FALSE}

ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(size = 0.5) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("darkorange", "darkorchid", "cyan4"), name = "Penguin Species")+
  labs(title = "Palmer Penguins' Flipper Length",
       subtitle = "Three species observed on three islands in the Palmer
       Archipelago", x = "Flipper Length (mm)", y = "Number of Penguins") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust =1), legend.position = "none") +
  coord_flip()

```

Awesome! Let's take a look at flipper length and it's relationship to body mass

```{r, message=FALSE}

ggplot(data = penguins_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species, shape = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(1,2,13))

```

Cool! Let's add species to this plot. What about island?
